sentences.text: Minqaria was a bird-hipped dinosaur belonging to the duck-billed family Hadrosauridae.
This genus contains only one known species, Minqaria bata, which is defined by a single partial skull.
Adult individuals of this species were estimated to reach a length of 3.5 meters and a mass of 250 kilograms.
Despite its small size, the fused bones of the braincase indicate that the holotype specimen was fully mature.
The fossil was preserved in nearshore marine phosphate deposits, a rare environment for terrestrial dinosaur remains.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as MHNM.KHG.1395, was discovered in the Sidi Chennane locality within the Oulad Abdoun Basin of Morocco.
Longrich and colleagues formally described Minqaria bata as a new genus and species in 2024.
To date, only one fossil occurrence of this dinosaur has been recorded in the scientific database.
Hypotheses for how these animals reached Africa include swimming, drifting, or rafting on floating debris, though rafting is considered unlikely for large adults but possible for juveniles.
Fossil evidence suggests that hadrosaurs were diverse and abundant in the Late Cretaceous Moroccan ecosystem, with specimens of various sizes found locally.
During the Late Cretaceous, Minqaria coexisted with its close relative Ajnabia, the predator Chenanisaurus, and sauropods.
Geological context suggests that Morocco may have been an isolated island during the time Minqaria lived.
Phylogenetic analysis places Minqaria within the hadrosaurid clade Arenysaurini, alongside Ajnabia and other Moroccan lambeosaurines.
Minqaria bata lived in Africa during the Late Cretaceous, specifically within the Maastrichtian stage from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
This places the animal approximately one million years before the K-Pg extinction event.
While Laurasia was characterized by tyrannosaurs and ceratopsians, Gondwana was dominated by titanosaurians and abelisaurians, as seen in Morocco.
Researchers consider oceanic dispersal the only viable explanation for how hadrosaurs like Minqaria reached Africa from Europe.
It remains debated whether intermittent land connections could have facilitated the dispersal of hadrosaurs to Africa alongside oceanic dispersal.
